title: Detection of Vulnerability Scanning
summary: This detection strategy covers active vulnerability scanning, where an adversary sends traffic to your internet facing systems to find weaknesses such as outdated software, weak authentication or exposed management interfaces. It differs from a broad port sweep because the goal is a specific flaw, so the traffic often includes protocol specific probes and malformed requests. The telemetry that makes it visible is firewall deny logs, intrusion detection alerts, web application firewall request records and honeypot logging. It fails in practice because scanning traffic is easily spread across many source addresses, and legitimate vulnerability management systems produce almost identical patterns.

beginner.definition: Vulnerability scanning means sending tests to a system to find a known weakness. The attacker looks for software that is out of date or badly configured. This is active work, so it leaves traces in your logs. This detection looks for many different probes against your public systems in a short time.
beginner.whyItMatters: Scanning is often the last quiet step before an attack. If you see it early, you can close the service or block the source. Many organisations find out only when the exploit succeeds, because they never watched their own edge. You also need to separate your own vulnerability management scans from hostile ones. That separation matters. Blocking your own scanner breaks your patching process. Ignoring a real scan leaves a door open. Good detection keeps both problems small.
howItWorks: Your firewall logs every denied connection with the source address, destination port and time.
Your intrusion detection system raises alerts when a request matches a known scanner pattern.
The detection counts how many distinct ports and hosts one source touches in a short window.
It compares that source with the address list used by your own vulnerability management system.
Web application firewall records are reviewed for probes against known vulnerable paths.
A source that probes many targets and is not an approved scanner raises an alert for triage.
beginner.example: Think of a night watchman who walks the fence line. He knows the electrician visits on Tuesdays and has a key. On Friday at midnight, somebody walks the same fence and tests every gate with a different tool. The watchman cannot see a crime yet, because the gates held. He writes down the time, the direction and the tools used. Your detection is that notebook. It records the walk along the fence. It also checks whether the visitor is the electrician or a stranger testing every gate.
takeaways: Scanning is active, so it always leaves evidence at your network edge.
Keep an accurate list of your own scanner addresses to avoid false alarms.
Many ports and many hosts from one source is the clearest pattern.

objectives: Define active vulnerability scanning and how it differs from a port sweep.
Identify the log sources at your network edge that record scanning.
Write a query that counts distinct ports and destinations per source.
Maintain an approved scanner address list for filtering.
Rank a scan alert against the other work in the queue.
dataSources: Firewall or edge router deny logs with source address, destination address, destination port and rule name
Intrusion detection or prevention alerts for scanner signatures and protocol anomalies
Web application firewall request records with path, method, user agent and response code
Honeypot or deception service logs on unused public addresses
Change records listing approved vulnerability management scanner addresses and scan windows
logic: The pattern is one source address contacting many destination ports or many destination hosts in a short period, especially with protocol specific or malformed requests rather than a completed session. The fields that must be correlated are the source address and its owning organisation, the count of distinct destination ports and destinations, the request paths and user agent in web logs, and the approved scanner address list held by the vulnerability management team. Benign cases include your own scheduled scans, hosted security services you subscribed to and content delivery health checks. The malicious case combines broad port coverage with targeted probes against a known vulnerable path, from a source that is not on the approved list and does not keep to a scan window.
pseudoQuery:
# title: Broad Port Scan Followed by Targeted Path Probes
# logsource:
#   product: network
# detection:
#   selection_scan:
#     action: 'deny'
#   filter_approved_scanners:
#     src_ip|in: 'approved_vulnerability_scanner_addresses'
#   condition: selection_scan and not filter_approved_scanners | count(distinct dst_port) by src_ip > 40
# level: medium
falsePositives: Your own vulnerability management platform when its scan window or address list changes.
A managed security service provider that scans from a new address range.
Availability monitoring services that check many ports after a configuration error.
A partner or customer testing their own connectivity against your public range.
tuningNotes: Keep the approved scanner list accurate and update it whenever the vulnerability management platform changes address, because a stale list is the main cause of noise here. Add filters for your monitoring providers and for partner test ranges. Scope the alerting rule to production public ranges and put development ranges into a daily summary. If you set the port threshold very high you lose the focused scan that only checks a handful of ports, so pair the broad rule with a second rule that alerts on probes to known vulnerable paths from any unapproved source.
